title: Given a singly linked list, reorder it so that the nodes interleave from the two ends: the first node, then the last, then the second, then the second-to-last, and so on. Do it in place. (LeetCode: Reorder List)
keyPoints: Three-step approach: find the middle with fast-slow pointers, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately
Linear time O(n) with constant extra space O(1) because only next pointers are rewired
Break the link between the first half's tail and the second half to prevent cycles
The merge alternates: take one from the first half, then one from the reversed second half
For odd-length lists, the first half is one node longer and the extra node terminates the chain
This is a direct composition of the midpoint and reversal building blocks

s1_definition.oneliner: Split at the middle, reverse the back half, then zip the two halves together alternately.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Reorder List** rearranges a linked list so nodes interleave from the front and back: first, last, second, second-to-last, and so on.
- **Three steps**: find the middle with fast-slow pointers, reverse the second half in place, then merge the two halves by alternating nodes.
- **In-place** means no new nodes are allocated; only existing `next` pointers are rewired.
- **Cycle prevention** requires breaking the link between the first half's tail and the second half before merging.
- **Complexity** is O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a chain of linked statement pages and wants to reorder them so the reader sees page one, then the last page, then page two, then the second-to-last, alternating inward from both ends. He finds the middle page, flips the back half around so it runs backward, and then zips the two halves together one page at a time, like shuffling two half-decks of cards into one.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reordering a linked list so nodes interleave from the front and back is a clean composition of three fundamental techniques: find the middle with fast-slow pointers, reverse the second half in place, and merge the two halves by alternating nodes. The naive approach copies every node into an array for random access, but the in-place approach rewires existing pointers in linear time with constant space.

The critical detail is the clean cut. After finding the middle, you must set the first half's tail next pointer to null before reversing and merging. Without this cut, the merge can wire the chain back into itself and create a cycle that causes infinite loops in any downstream traversal. This single line of code is the difference between a correct solution and a subtle production bug.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this in a statement presentation mode. A reviewer wanted the pages interleaved from the front and back so they could compare opening and closing pages as they scrolled. The statements could be long, so copying all the pages into an array was wasteful, and the in-place reorder rewired the existing chain without allocating anything.

The senior-level insight is that the same split-reverse-merge pattern appears in palindrome checks, list sorting, and list folding. Mastering the three building blocks separately and knowing how to compose them cleanly is what makes this family of problems manageable.

Remember one sentence: split at the middle, reverse the back half, merge alternately, and break the link to prevent cycles.
